A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same QG-SMS work. All 13 pages of v1 and 17 pages of v2, including their appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

before.justification: V1 reports original evaluations on EduAgent and DBE-KT, threshold and simulation-robustness analyses, and a three-annotator study covering 120 question pairs.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and adds baseline evaluations, an ablation of the final evaluation step, and a distractor-efficiency ranking experiment.

M1.justification: The three-step QG-SMS procedure and substantive prompts remain unchanged. V2 Section 5.2 implements a ranking extension that aggregates pairwise preferences into normalized question scores; v1 only suggested ranking as a possible extension.

E1.justification: The datasets, educational domains, and human/generated-question coverage are retained. V2 adds evaluation on EduAgent distractor-efficiency pairs with equal or small quality differences, extending the earlier setting restricted to clearly separated questions.

E2.justification: V2 adds QSalience, using its mistral-instruct model, to the individual-scoring comparisons in Section 4.2 and Table 2. BERTScore, KDA, and the six existing pairwise LLM baselines remain.

E3.justification: V2 adds a direct-statistics control and a 308-pair ranking evaluation using Spearman, Kendall, and Pearson correlations. The primary benchmark thresholds, GPT-4o checkpoint, order-swapping procedure, and human-study design remain unchanged. Expanded TC construction and API settings are newly documented details rather than established changes to existing experiments.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained threshold-sensitivity and five-run robustness analyses, v2 tests whether direct DF/DC calculations can replace the final LLM judgment and examines ranking without a minimum quality gap. Appendix A.4 also expands the existing computer-vision case with outputs from five baselines, substantially strengthening the diagnostic analyses.

E5.justification: V2 introduces pairwise binomial significance tests against Vanilla, full p-values in Table 6, and p < 0.1 annotations in Table 2. The ranking study adds group means and standard deviations and an ANOVA test. The existing five-run robustness plot is retained; no increase in repetitions is established.

E6.justification: Shared post-examination and human-study scores are unchanged. V2 adds detailed TC results, including DBE-KT and individual-scoring results, QSalience scores, ranking results, and baseline response examples. The new ablation reports direct calculation changing DF accuracy from 68.55 to 73.11 and DC from 66.39 to 56.83; Table 4 reports QG-SMS ranking correlations of 0.48, 0.38, and 0.50.

T1.justification: The original item-statistic definitions and quality-gap condition remain unchanged. V2 Section 5.2 adds a mathematical definition of the ranking score: credit 1 for preference in both orders or 0.5 in one order, then normalize by the question's pair count. No theorems or proofs are added.

C1.justification: The abstract and three principal contribution statements retain the same claims: introduce test-item analysis into QG evaluation, propose single-LLM student modeling and simulation, and demonstrate effectiveness and robustness. Added evidence and future applications do not redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive arguments about the necessity of the final LLM step and applicability to similar-quality questions, and revises baseline reliability interpretations by dimension. It also proposes long-context distraction as a baseline failure mechanism, acknowledges the p < 0.1 significance threshold, and discusses reward-based optimization and research-question evaluation as future applications.

D1.justification: V2 materially expands reproducibility information with a QG-SMS implementation link, detailed TC pair construction, use of all generated profiles without filtering, default GPT-4o settings and temperature 1 for robustness runs, and QSalience implementation and scoring details. The GPT-4o checkpoint and minimum-ten-profile prompt were already disclosed in v1.

R1.justification: V2 expands comparisons with prior student-simulation research, including artificial crowds and manually controlled profiles, and removes the statement that earlier approaches overlook discrimination and distractor efficiency. Additional citations support QSalience, profile-count selection, and future applications, while the central single-LLM, automatically generated-profile positioning remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, main section sequence, and much of the prose remain intact. V2 rewrites selected baseline, results, related-work, and conclusion passages, moves scoring-direction details into Appendix A.2, and adds Appendix A.4. These are localized expansions rather than a document-wide restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 converts the introductory case illustration into a text table, redraws the overview performance plot with grouped markers and a zero-based axis, and substantially enlarges and redesigns both prompt figures. It also expands the main results table and adds ranking, significance, and qualitative-analysis tables.

improvement.justification: V2 makes the study easier to assess and reproduce through the final-step ablation, ranking validation, explicit statistical tests, fuller baseline comparisons, and implementation information. The improvement is limited by overinterpretation: direct calculation improves difficulty accuracy, while Table 6 shows neither discrimination gain over Vanilla meets the stated significance threshold. These findings warrant more qualification than the retained broad superiority and new necessity claims provide.
